opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The key is that an IMO proof and a research-level proof are very different objects.

An Olympiad solution is maybe one or two pages. A strong human grader can read it in a few minutes and decide whether it's right. So when a model writes a natural-language proof for an IMO problem, verification is cheap. You can have human judges, or even another model, check it, and you'll be fairly confident.

Professional mathematics doesn't work like that. A serious research paper might run fifty, a hundred, sometimes several hundred pages. It builds on dozens of earlier papers, each with its own lemmas, conventions, and occasionally hidden gaps. Even among human experts, refereeing a major result can take months or years, and errors still slip through. Think of the long checking process for Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem, the years spent digesting Mochizuki's work on abc, or the cases where published theorems later turned out to have flaws. Human verification is already the bottleneck for human mathematicians.

Now imagine AI producing mathematics at scale: thousands of long, plausible-looking proofs. Language models are very good at producing text that *looks* rigorous. A subtle error on page 37, a step that says "by a standard argument" when no such argument exists, a quantifier quietly swapped. These are exactly the mistakes that are hardest for a tired human referee to catch. Without a reliable checker, we'd be flooded with output we can't trust, and mathematics without trust is worthless. Its whole value is certainty.

That's where Lean comes in. In a formal system like Lean, every step is checked mechanically by a small, trusted kernel. If the proof compiles, it's correct relative to the stated definitions and axioms, full stop. The cost of verification drops from months of expert attention to minutes of computer time. Then the human effort can focus on the part that really needs judgment: are the definitions and the theorem statement what we actually mean? Is this result interesting?

There's a second reason, beyond checking. Formal verification gives AI a clean, unambiguous reward signal. For reinforcement learning, "did it compile and prove the goal" is an almost ideal feedback signal. It can't be gamed by persuasive prose. That lets models explore, fail, and improve on genuinely hard problems in a way natural-language training can't fully support. It's similar to how AlphaGo benefited from having a perfectly defined game: Lean turns mathematics into an environment where correctness is precisely defined.

And Lean, through Mathlib, is building a shared, machine-readable library of mathematics, a foundation that both humans and AI can build on reliably, instead of each new result relying on everyone re-reading everything.

So my view isn't that natural-language reasoning is unimportant. Intuition, high-level ideas, and informal sketches are where creativity lives, and models are getting remarkably good at that. But to go from "a model that can solve competition problems" to "a model whose new theorems mathematicians can actually rely on," you need a verification layer that scales with the output. For now, formal systems like Lean are the most credible path to that.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts short Olympiad solutions with long research proofs and their verification costs, but does not distinguish creative problem solving from relatively limited mathematical knowledge.

r002.rationale: It says language models can produce plausible-looking text with subtle errors and argues that natural-language proofs need a reliable checker, conveying that complex proofs in prose cannot be guaranteed correct.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention Peter Scholze or describe Lean being used to resolve doubts about his proof.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short answer is that Olympiad problems and research mathematics are different kinds of objects, and the thing that makes natural-language proofs acceptable for one breaks down for the other.

An IMO problem is short, self-contained, and has a known answer. The proof is maybe a page or two. A human grader can read it in twenty minutes and tell you whether it is right. So when a model produces a natural-language IMO proof, verification is cheap, and the risk of a subtle error slipping through is low. The whole pipeline still rests on a human checking the output, but that check is tractable.

Research mathematics is nothing like that. A real paper might be fifty or a hundred pages. It builds on a tower of prior results, each with its own hypotheses, and the places where things go wrong are almost never the big ideas. They are the boundary cases, the lemma that was stated for compact spaces but got applied to something non-compact, the constant that was supposed to be independent of n but quietly isn't. Expert referees miss these all the time. There are published results that stood for years before someone found the gap.

Now imagine a model producing that kind of mathematics at scale. The model is very good at writing text that looks like a proof. It has read every textbook and paper. And that is exactly the danger, because its errors will be the plausible kind, the kind that pattern-match to correct arguments. If the only verifier is a human reading prose, the human becomes the bottleneck, and a tired human reading the fiftieth page is not a reliable instrument. You end up with a system that generates confident mathematics faster than anyone can check it, and some fraction of it is wrong in ways nobody notices. That is worse than useless for a working mathematician, because the one thing you need from a proof is that it is actually true.

Lean changes the economics of that. Once a proof is formalized and the kernel accepts it, verification is done. It does not matter how long the proof is or how much it leans on earlier results, because those were checked too. You can let the model try ten thousand approaches, fail on most of them, and only surface the ones that compile. The human no longer has to trust the model's output. They only have to trust the statement of the theorem and a very small kernel that has been scrutinized for years. That is a completely different trust relationship.

There is also a second benefit people underrate. When a model works in Lean, it gets a precise signal at every step. Natural-language reasoning gives you no feedback until a human reads it. Lean tells you immediately that this rewrite failed, this goal is not closed, this hypothesis is missing. For training and for search, that signal is enormously valuable. It is the difference between learning with a teacher and learning by guessing.

So I would put it this way. Natural language is fine for communicating mathematics between people who can check each other. For a machine producing mathematics that a professional would actually build on, you need something a machine can check, and today that means a proof assistant. Lean happens to be the one with the best library and the most momentum, which is why it has become the natural choice.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between producing a proof that sounds convincing and producing a proof we can reliably verify. A model can write a very fluent mathematical argument, but there may be a gap hidden in one step. And when the argument is long or involves unfamiliar mathematics, finding that gap can require a great deal of work from a professional mathematician.

The Olympiad is a useful benchmark, but its problems are designed to have relatively short, self-contained solutions. Research mathematics can involve many layers of definitions and results. Success on Olympiad problems doesn’t automatically tell us that a model can manage those dependencies reliably.

Lean gives us a way to make the verification explicit. You state the theorem formally, and every step of the proof has to satisfy a precise set of rules. The model can propose an argument, but the proof checker decides whether that argument actually establishes the stated result. That also gives the model feedback it can use to revise its attempt.

I wouldn’t say Lean is the only possible system, or that formal verification alone makes an AI a mathematician. Choosing interesting questions and discovering useful ideas are still essential. But if we want AI to produce mathematics at scale, we need a way to check its work without asking a human expert to scrutinize every line. That’s the role I see Lean playing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key distinction is between producing a proof that looks convincing and producing a proof that we can reliably verify. An IMO problem is very difficult, but it is also relatively self-contained. The statement is short, the background is fairly standard, and a human can usually check the proposed solution without reconstructing an entire research program.

At the research level, a proof may depend on many definitions and theorems, each with very specific assumptions. A model can write a very fluent argument while quietly missing a condition or making a circular inference. And as the argument gets longer, those mistakes become harder to detect. If a mathematician has to check every step, that becomes a bottleneck.

Lean makes those obligations explicit. You give it a precise statement and a proof, and its kernel checks whether the proof follows from the definitions and assumptions. So the AI can propose ideas, make mistakes, and revise them, while getting a reliable signal about whether an argument actually works.

That doesn’t mean formal verification replaces mathematical creativity. You still need to choose interesting questions and discover useful ideas. And Lean verifies the statement you actually formalized, so getting that statement right matters too. But I see it as essential infrastructure for scaling AI mathematics: we need a way to build long arguments on results we can trust, rather than just accumulate plausible-looking text.
